question: 26.2 % of women in the EU live with some form of disability1 and experience intersectional discrimination. They are more exposed to poverty and unemployment, as only 20 % work full-time and only 16 % report good health, compared to 50 % and 83 %, respectively, of women without disabilities.2 At the same time, forced sterilisation of women with disabilities is prohibited in only nine Member States.

3 However, the new Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030 does not effectively address these multiple discriminations, as it does not include binding actions and largely ignores the situation of women and girls with disabilities.

Having regard to: - the recent statement of the European Disability Forum (EDF), which condemned the fact that the new strategy is limited to a few general references to disability, without substantive measures to address the needs of people with disabilities4, - the provisions of the UNCRPD5, - Article 39 of the Istanbul Convention, which explicitly prohibits forced sterilisation, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend to put in place additional initiatives and measures for women and girls with disabilities, with the aim of ensuring reasonable adjustments, enhancing access to health, employment and inclusive education and prohibiting the practice of forced sterilisation within the Union?
Does it intend to develop gender-disaggregated indicators of progress on the rights of persons with disabilities, in line with the UNCRPD, as requested by the European Parliament in its resolution?

Eurostat, hlth_silc_12. Gender Equality Index 2025, EIGE, employment and health sectors. EDF, Forced sterilisation of persons with disabilities in the EU, 09/2022. According to EDF, the new strategy does not address the forced sterilization of women and girls with disabilities, a serious violation of human rights and the CFTEU, which continues to exist in many European countries.

Women with disabilities are mentioned only in the Strategy, mainly in general terms. A brief reference is made in the introduction, while in Principle 2 the obstacles to health are recognized, in Principle 5 the increased employment gap and in Principle 6 the difficulties in education, but without any specific measures, actions or political initiatives are foreseen.
See UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, in particular Article 6 ‘Women with Disabilities’.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20301 sets out measures to advance gender equality for women and men in all their diversity, including women with disabilities. In implementing the Strategy, specific barriers faced by women and girls with disabilities will be addressed.

Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence2 ensures that victims of forms of violence against women criminalised under EU or national law can benefit from the support services and redress mechanisms provided for in the Directive. This also includes victims of forced sterilisation where such conduct is criminalised under national law.

In the enhanced strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities3, the Commission commits to issuing guidance on the employment of women with disabilities and assessing the provision of reasonable accommodation at the workplace4. Ways to improve quality and accessibility of women’s physical and mental healthcare will be further explored with the World Health Organization5.

This builds on recent initiatives, such as the EU4Health Programme project on improving access to care for people with disabilities6. The Commission will launch a study on violence against women with disabilities and will facilitate the development of guidelines on procedural accommodation for victims with disabilities.

To improve the disaggregation of data on all grounds of discrimination, the Commission is preparing a Recommendation on equality data to help Member States and other stakeholders to monitor the state of equality in the EU.
